paragraphs.heading: Breaking a polynomial into pieces
paragraphs.text: Factoring a polynomial means writing it as a product of irreducible factors, keeping the coefficients in the same number system the polynomial started in. That system may be the integers or a field, such as the rational, real or complex numbers. A polynomial is irreducible when it is not the product of two non-constant polynomials.

paragraphs.heading: Always possible, always the same
paragraphs.text: For polynomials over the integers or over a field, such a breakdown always exists: each one is a constant times a product of irreducible polynomials. The breakdown is also unique, apart from multiplying the factors by invertible constants. In technical terms, such polynomial rings are called unique factorization domains.

paragraphs.heading: It depends on the numbers allowed
paragraphs.text: What counts as fully factored depends on the base field. Over the complex numbers, the fundamental theorem of algebra says every polynomial with complex coefficients has complex roots. So a polynomial with integer coefficients splits completely into linear, or first-degree, factors there. Over the real numbers, no irreducible factor has degree higher than two, but over the rationals there are irreducible polynomials of every degree.

paragraphs.heading: A job for computers
paragraphs.text: Polynomial factorization is a core part of computer algebra systems. Modern algorithms can quickly factor one-variable polynomials of degree above 1000 whose coefficients run to thousands of digits. A basic step, even for rational coefficients, is factoring over a finite field. The question only makes sense when every coefficient can be stored in a computer and there are algorithms for arithmetic on them, and even then Fröhlich and Shepherdson found fields where no factoring algorithm can exist.

paragraphs.heading: Integers and fractions
paragraphs.text: Factoring over the rationals and over the integers is essentially the same problem. The content of a polynomial with integer coefficients is, up to sign, the greatest common divisor of its coefficients, and dividing by it leaves the primitive part. Gauss showed that multiplying two primitive polynomials always gives a primitive one, a result called Gauss's lemma. It follows that a primitive polynomial is irreducible over the rationals exactly when it is irreducible over the integers.

paragraphs.heading: Clearing out repeated factors
paragraphs.text: If a factor appears twice, the polynomial is a multiple of that factor's square, and the factor also divides the polynomial's derivative. For one-variable polynomials over the rationals, Yun's algorithm uses this to split a polynomial into square-free factors, ones that are not a multiple of a square. It does so with a chain of greatest common divisor steps, starting with gcd(f(x), f '(x)). After that it is enough to factor each square-free piece, which is why this is the first step in most factoring algorithms.

paragraphs.heading: Methods for pencil and paper
paragraphs.text: Textbooks teach some methods that are handy when working by hand. Computers skip them because they rely on factoring integers, which is currently slower than factoring polynomials. One example is the rational root test, which finds every linear factor with rational coefficients.
